extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literature and aesthetics; educated general readers interested in Goethe and literary criticism (also readers interested in history of astronomy/observational practice in the earlier essay section)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical/analytical guidance on what makes a great poet (Goethe) and accompanying discussion of practical criteria for mountain observatories and coronal photography. The page articulates aesthetic standards (qualities of the 'sovereign poet', measures of completeness, didactic function, vocation/self-culture, etc.) and practical/technical criteria for astronomical observation at high altitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign poet: combination of poetical and philosophical qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: “The highest rank in literature belongs to those who combine the properly poetical with philosophical qualities, and crown both with a certain robust sincerity and common sense.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sovereign poet must be not merely a singer but also a sage: to passion and music he must add large ideas; he must extend in width as well as in height; he must not be a dreamer or fanatic and must be rooted in the hard earth. This is given as the defining standard for first‑rank literature (Goethe, Dante, Shakespeare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness in three dimensions (feeling, knowledge, grasp of reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Of this trio each is complete in all the three dimensions. Each feels deeply, each knows and sees clearly, and each has a stout grasp of reality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universal/lasting literary fame rests on the combination of deep feeling, clear knowledge/insight, and a robust grasp of reality. Deficit in any one dimension reduces completeness (examples: Dante less rational; Shakespeare lacking academic knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacherliness/systematic unity (having a theory of life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe is distinguished from other greats by being ‘essentially much more of a teacher’ and by having ‘a system, a theory of life, which he has thought and worked out for himself.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being a teacher (didactic element) and having an underlying system or principle that unifies one’s works is a mark of high rank. Unity may be obscured by variety of subjects and styles, but the root principle should be present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility must not be mere talent or mimicry
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Goethe’s writings show a ‘mastery of so many literary styles’, versatility alone should not be taken as evidence of genius; Goethe’s versatility is not 'a mocking-bird' imitation but genuine artistic breadth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should distinguish between mere facility/talent (imitation) and authentic genius that uses versatility to explore and express genuine insights. Beware the anti‑pattern of calling multiplicity of styles proof only of facile talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity beneath multiplicity (variety may hide unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe has a centre (unity) though 'the variety of his subjects and styles is so great... that the unity is much less obvious than the multiplicity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a large oeuvre, look for an organizing principle or root view even if styles and subjects vary widely; do not mistake surface diversity for lack of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctness and character; resolute clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe admired 'distinctness, character' and struggled 'for clearness' against national vagueness; he valued resolute acts of choice to attain definite opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary greatness includes having definite, clear views (character) rather than diffuse tolerance or vagueness. The ability and will to choose and clarify is a positive criterion; the anti‑pattern is facile universal impartiality and indecision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of mere indifferent quietism — preoccupation with a central task
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent quietism or aloofness should be read as preoccupation: Goethe 'had prescribed to himself in early life a task, and he declined to be drawn aside from it by the controversies of the time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate detachment from contemporary controversies with indifference; assess whether an author’s apparent aloofness results from a sustained, serious project. Value sustained commitment to a self‑imposed intellectual/life task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-culture / making one's existence harmonious
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe’s central task is 'self-culture' — 'to develop completely all that is in me' and 'to make my own existence harmonious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should recognise self-culture (systematic self-development and harmonising life) as a legitimate moral/aesthetic aim. It is not necessarily selfish; it can be a disciplined experiment in conduct with public relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure conceived as energetic activity and imaginative creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe redefines 'pleasure' as not passive sensation but 'energetic action' — 'the most necessary of all pleasures to him is that of imaginative creation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In judging a life or work, value active, creative satisfaction (productive pleasures) over mere passive sensual gratification. Creative work as a central source of 'satisfaction of desire' is a positive criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to aimless self-denial (critique of abstinence divorced from ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Goethe attacks 'the timid superstition which sets up self-denial, divorced from all rational ends, as a thing good and right in itself' and protests against self-denial 'which leads to nothing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral or aesthetic systems should not praise self-denial for its own sake; assess whether abstinence is purposive (serves a greater end) rather than mere stagnation. Anti-pattern: valorising mortification when it yields no benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of self-knowledge and vocation for human happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal condition of happiness is 'a just self-knowledge' — 'He will be happy, who knows what he wants and what he can do.' Goethe emphasises discovering one's true vocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating characters, authors, or educational aims, give weight to work that promotes self-knowledge and guidance toward vocation. Criticises education that 'excites wishes, instead of awakening tastes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: The novel as vehicle for views of life (Wilhelm Meister model)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Wilhelm Meister’ is presented as the first important novel dealing 'principally and on a large scale with opinions or views of life' — the novel as a text‑book of Goethian philosophy and vocational development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novels for their ability to handle ideas about life and vocation seriously; measure instructiveness and practical moral inquiry, not merely adventure/entertainment. Consider influence: the novel that teaches can reshape the form of the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for judging didactic novels: seriousness, instructiveness, moral distinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the didactic elements are 'seriously instructive', whether the moral of the story is convincingly brought out, and whether instruction is balanced with interest (criticising 'Wilhelm Meister' as 'seldom very amusing' and sometimes not 'convincing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A didactic novel should instruct without being dull; its moral or lesson should be presented with clarity and conviction. Beware one‑sided innovations that ignore orthodox virtues or swing to extremes and alienate conservative readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential method for photographing the corona
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Huggins’s method 'may be described as a differential one'—it 'depends for its success on the superior intensity of coronal to ordinary sunlight in the extreme violet region' and on the fact that 'chloride of silver is sensitive to those rays only in which the corona is strongest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical evaluators should recognise that coronal photography relies on spectral selectivity (violet excess) and photographic chemistry. Practical success requires exploiting that spectral advantage to separate coronal image from solar glare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of great altitudes for celestial photography and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The advantages of great altitudes can hardly be exaggerated’ — finer air reduces glare and atmospheric ravages especially of violet rays; 'the proportion... of short and quick vibrations in the light received becomes exalted as we press upwards.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Site selection and operational planning for solar physics, stellar spectroscopy, and celestial photography should prioritize high altitude to maximize transmission of short-wavelength light and reduce atmospheric disturbance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mountain observatory site selection: avoid persistent cloud/vapor-condensers
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Not all elevated points are available... Some act persistently as vapor-condensers, and seldom doff their sullen cap of clouds. From any mountain in the United Kingdom, for instance, it would be folly to expect an astronomical benefit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing a station, evaluate local meteorology (cloud frequency, vapor condensation) and not just altitude. Examples: Ben Nevis may be meteorologically poor despite height; high but cloudy sites are unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human and logistical drawbacks of extreme altitude observatories
rubrics_metrics.description: High altitudes bring storms, violent winds, intense solar radiation and cold, physiological effects ('The head aches; the pulse throbs; every inspiration is a gasp for breath'), cooking and fuel problems ('difficulty of cooking with water that boils... below 212°; fires reluctant to burn; tobacco not to keep alight').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance scientific gains against practical human costs: staffing, seasonality, risk to health, and logistical difficulty (cooking, heating). Expect a probationary acclimatization period and reduced labor efficiency even when acclimatised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical altitude recommendations and seasonality
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Copeland recommends occupation during the most favourable season (say October to December) of an 'extra-elevated station' at 18,500 ft for particular purposes; for a permanent mountain observatory '12,500 ft would be the outside limit of practical usefulness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan temporary high‑altitude campaigns for optimal seasons and limit permanent installations to lower altitudes (≈12,500 ft) to balance observational advantage with human/operational practicality. Consider regional alternatives (Rocky Mountains vs Andes).
